articles.title: Halfway is a place to ask better questions
articles.dek: Two unbeaten teams, a receiver with 755 yards, and several defenses waiting for help. Ellis Quill picks his midseason standouts and revisits what PSPN thought it knew.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: The calendar has reached its midpoint. The teams have not all played the same number of games, which is a useful first warning against pretending that halfway means everything is conveniently comparable. This is an eighteen-week, seventeen-game season. Mossdeep and Mt. Silver have played eight and won eight. Sunyshore and Cinnabar have played nine and won seven. There is enough evidence to have opinions, and enough football left for those opinions to become embarrassing.

I would like to keep both facts in view. A midseason column should be more than an awards list delivered with the confidence of a court order. It should ask what we have learned, what we have mistaken for learning, and which questions will still matter when the last bye is over. Some of our strongest answers concern teams that have earned attention. Others concern teams that have made the same disappointment look different each week.
Start with the people who keep changing the score

My midseason most valuable player is Dram Marino. These are my selections, not league honors. Marino has 2,068 passing yards, twenty-five touchdown passes and two interceptions through eight games. Mossdeep's running game is excellent enough that a quarterback could disappear into the collective success. Marino has instead made the collective success much easier to sustain. Against Cerulean he completed seventeen of twenty, threw three touchdowns and took no sacks. That is a fairly persuasive way to return from a week off.

Ninjaskamara is my offensive player of the first half: 953 rushing yards, eighteen rushing touchdowns, and another 274 receiving yards with three receiving scores. The five-touchdown afternoon against Cerulean was the loudest recent installment, not the whole case. I am giving the quarterback the broader award and the running back this one because both have earned a serious conversation. Anyone who reverses those choices has numbers with which to argue. I will listen, though probably after finishing my sentence.

My defensive choice is Verrick Brooks. Thirteen sacks in seven appearances remain thirteen sacks while he is injured. The absence matters enormously to Saffron's future; it does not remove the first-half work. Canalave's Passimian and Cinnabar's Arcanine each have eight sacks. Viridian's Sigilyph leads the interception list with six and just helped create a late opportunity against Dewford. The race is open, especially with Brooks still out three weeks. My ballot is a photograph of the work so far, not a reservation for the final award.

The receiving story belongs in more than one city. Vermilion's Drakloak leads with 755 yards. Accel BeckhmJr has 659 and eleven receiving touchdowns for Mossdeep; HeeDee Lamb has 631 for Saffron, with Gengar Pickens at 592. Production can arrive in different shapes. Drakloak's yardage should not vanish because the Volts have a narrow point differential. BeckhmJr's scoring should not be treated as an automatic byproduct of wearing a winning jersey. Each has given his team something substantial.
The strongest teams still have questions

Mossdeep's question is becoming more interesting than whether it can beat the next struggling defense. The Eclipse have outscored opponents 363–59, yet their 24–21 win at Dewford remains a useful part of the record. A close game is possible. Saffron arrives next, followed by a remaining schedule that includes Rustboro, Petalburg, Canalave and Sunyshore. The first half has earned Mossdeep confidence. The second half will ask it to carry that confidence through different kinds of resistance.

Mt. Silver has allowed 68 points and survived losing Josh Alakazam. In Week 6 I argued that Crem did not need to become his injured predecessor. That remains my view. The Reds' Week 8 win over Snowpoint included a kickoff-return touchdown and an interception return for a touchdown, helping cover two interceptions thrown. Connor McLarren has built a team capable of distributing the responsibility. The question is how often the other departments can keep repairing the same error before an opponent stops offering another chance.

Saffron's defense has allowed fifty points, the lowest total among these contenders, and now faces Mossdeep without Brooks or Ninetales. Blackthorn is 7–1 after another win. Sunyshore has reached 7–2 by recovering from a 12–6 loss at Cerulean with two victories. Cinnabar is also 7–2 and just answered the question of whether its recent defensive control could travel into a game with a winning Petalburg side. These teams do not need identical labels. They need their next difficult possession to go well.
What our own pages got right, and what they owe another look

Rowan placed Eterna eighth last week after moving it up six spots. Mara's column argued that the Thorns made opponents earn the last yard. Eterna followed with a 20–6 win at Cianwood and now has allowed 64 points in eight games. The encouraging change is on the other side: nineteen and twenty points in successive wins after losses in which the offense scored six, six and three. We should recognize a defense that has been doing its job, while watching whether the offense's recent help continues.

Last week I wrote about Fortree finally getting a different question after its first win. The Skyhawks answered with a 24–20 victory at Fuchsia. Two wins do not erase six defeats or the injuries now affecting the roster. They do make it harder to treat the opening losing streak as a complete description of Winona's team. This is the sort of modest revision that a season demands: change the opinion by the amount the evidence supports, without pretending a new week requires a new identity.

Lavender needs the same patience, but patience cannot become an excuse to ignore repetition. The Wails were competitive at Blackthorn and level at halftime against Sunyshore, then lost both. At 4–4 they remain in a current playoff place with a minus-75 point differential. I am sympathetic to the difference between a bad stretch and a bad team. I am also waiting for a second half that gives the distinction some practical value.

The most useful disappointment to discuss is not a team failing expectations we never recorded. It is a team failing the opportunities visible in front of it. Fuchsia has one win in nine games despite Empoleon's 1,932 passing yards. That disconnect is a real question. So is Vermilion's six wins with only eight more points scored than allowed. One club needs production to become wins; the other needs its wins to acquire a sturdier foundation.

The next nine weeks will not settle every argument at once. Saffron at Mossdeep, Mt. Silver at Canalave and Cinnabar at Rustboro will begin to sharpen several of them immediately. I would rather arrive at those games with an opinion I can revise than a slogan I have to protect. Halfway is a good place to celebrate the work. It is an even better place to stop confusing the work already done with the work still owed.

articles.title: Forty-seven seconds is enough if you stop apologizing
articles.dek: Dewford surrendered the lead, then drove to the tying field goal and won in overtime. Mara Voss wants Brawly to keep the response and fix the reason it was needed.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: I don't want to hear that Dewford wanted this game more. I want to hear about the throws. With forty-seven seconds left in regulation, Viridian had a 17–14 lead and the Breakers had the ball at their own eighteen after the kickoff return. Dewford reached a 28-yard field goal with eight seconds left and eventually won 23–17 in overtime. Desire is difficult to chart. The completions are right there.

Frosmoth threw incomplete deep right, then found Swellow short right for thirteen yards. Another incompletion followed. Then came thirty yards to Ambipom deep right, seventeen to Loudred deep right, two more incompletions, and eleven to Bayleef short right on third-and-ten. Numel made the tying kick. That is an offense using the available clock without treating every failed pass as a reason to abandon the next useful decision. I want Brawly to preserve that clarity. I also want him to stop needing it quite so often.
The situation was partly self-inflicted

Dewford had led 14–9. Frosmoth then threw an interception to Sigilyph with 2:30 remaining. Viridian turned the opportunity into a thirteen-play, 80-yard touchdown drive, with Dewott scoring from eight yards and converting the two-point try. The Breakers' late response deserves praise. The interception still deserves criticism. These are compatible positions, despite the amount of energy football discussions spend pretending otherwise.

There had also been a first-half fumble by Kricketune, recovered by Viridian's Stunfisk. Dewford finished with two turnovers to Viridian's none. This is not a detail to hide underneath the overtime result. When an offense produces 375 yards, converts five of eight third downs and still needs a kick in the last ten seconds to remain alive, the discarded possessions are part of the explanation. The Breakers had enough production to make winning easier. They repeatedly made it harder.

Last week Rowan liked Dewford's recovery to 4–4 while asking it to stop requiring forgiveness. The wording was amusing; the concern was accurate. Now the Breakers are 5–4 and still conducting an unusually thorough examination of how much forgiveness a rushing game can purchase. Ambipom carried twenty times for 122 yards and caught four passes for another 53. That is 175 yards of useful work. It should buy more than a weekly audition for the rescue squad.

body.speaker: Ambipom
body.text: If you want the drive to keep going, give me something to do. I don't mind the late work. I'd prefer we didn't spend the first part of the game making extra work for ourselves.
There was more than one response worth keeping

Viridian's first touchdown came with 1:17 left in the second quarter, a three-yard pass from Mr. Rime to Dewott. Dewford answered at 0:54 with a 56-yard deep-left touchdown pass from Frosmoth to Swellow on third-and-four. That was not the same kind of drive as the late field-goal march. It was a single large completion at a moment when the opponent had just scored. The Breakers have shown they can respond quickly. The next step is keeping that response from becoming their entire personality.

The fourth-quarter touchdown to Pidgeotto was different again: a ten-yard short-left completion with 4:12 remaining. Dewford had multiple ways to reach the end zone before the interception put its lead in danger. Frosmoth finished fifteen-of-twenty-six for 235 yards, two passing touchdowns and a pick, then supplied the one-yard rushing touchdown that won overtime. That is enough good quarterback work to discuss in detail, and enough bad ball placement to demand a correction without turning the whole performance into an indictment.

I am deliberately separating the throw from the outcome. A deep attempt can fail and still leave the offense with a sound next decision. A completion can be too short to solve the down. On the last regulation drive, the eleven-yard pass to Bayleef on third-and-ten was useful precisely because it cleared the needed distance. Those yards moved Dewford toward a makeable field goal. They were not merely a completion to make the passing line look friendlier.

body.speaker: Brawly
body.text: We had to get enough ground for a real chance at the kick. The players stayed with that. We also have to look at why we were chasing the game in the first place. Winning doesn't make those possessions disappear.
Viridian helped create its own problem

The Titans deserve credit for taking the late lead. Mr. Rime's drive included a 22-yard deep-left completion to Delibird on third-and-six and a fourteen-yard short-right completion to Loudred on third-and-seven. Those were substantial conversions under pressure, not a defense simply watching the clock expire. Dewott then finished the touchdown and the two-point try. Giovanni's offense did the difficult work necessary to move ahead.

What it could not do was make the remaining time irrelevant. Dewford's late completions repeatedly gained enough distance to sustain the attempt. The Titans finished with only three successful third downs in eleven tries, compared with Dewford's five in eight, and punted five times. They had the lead late because their best possession arrived at a useful moment. Their full-game offense had not created enough separation to survive the visitor's answer.

Gabite ran nineteen times for 87 yards, while Mr. Rime completed sixteen of twenty-four for 130 yards. Those are contributions, but the passing game needed more than a modest average gain when it finally had to keep pace. The Titans are 4–5 after consecutive home losses to Rustboro and Dewford. A week ago they traveled ninety yards on a possession without scoring before halftime. This week they scored late and still left enough time. The details differ; the unfinished work persists.

Dewford's narrow Week 4 loss to Mossdeep remains a useful comparison. The Breakers can play close games against strong opposition. That does not make every close game evidence of hidden greatness, and beating a 4–4 Viridian side in overtime does not make the turnovers harmless. It establishes a more limited, more valuable point: this offense can recover within a game when it continues making specific, workable decisions.

The Breakers enter their bye above .500. Unfezant remains listed out one week, and there is time to review the possessions that forced the dramatic ending. Keep Ambipom's useful workload. Keep the willingness to find a completion that actually reaches the line to gain. Keep the composure after an incompletion. Then remove the unnecessary invitations. Forty-seven seconds was enough this time. Brawly should be pleased with the answer and irritated by the question.

articles.title: Six wins. Eight points. Explain the difference.
articles.dek: Vermilion owns a 6–2 record and a plus-eight point differential. Dorian Pike finds one excellent closing drive—and a team that needs to make that drive its standard.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: I would like to congratulate Lt. Surge on six wins. Six actual, permanent, available-for-inspection wins. Nobody is repossessing them because the point differential is awkward. Vermilion is 6–2, occupies a current playoff position and just beat Lavaridge 24–17. That is the respectful opening. Please enjoy it while it lasts.

The Volts have scored 116 points and allowed 108. Eight points separate the season totals. Eight. A 6–2 record usually arrives wearing a larger coat than that. This one is standing at the door insisting it does not feel the draft. The record is real. So is the amount of room Vermilion has left between a successful first half and a rather less reassuring explanation of how it happened.

And here's the uncomfortable truth: the best argument for this team is not the record on its own. It is the last possession against Lavaridge. Ten plays, 58 yards, the final 4:08 removed from the game. No additional points. No opportunity for the opponent. That is the version of Vermilion I want to see promoted from occasional appearance to regular employment.
The drive that earned the applause

Lavaridge had cut the lead to seven with 4:14 remaining. After the kickoff, Vermilion began at its own twenty-one. Kangaskhan gained nothing up the middle, then six yards to the left. On third-and-five, Chandelure threw short left to Swalot for ten. The clock continued moving because the offense had completed the actual task. Not a decorative catch. A first down.

Chandelure went back to Swalot for six, then found Galvantula short middle for eleven on second-and-four. After the two-minute warning, a six-yard completion to Volbeat and a five-yard throw to Victreebel produced another first down. Then Ariados caught a sixteen-yard deep-left pass. Two kneels finished the afternoon. Lt. Surge, that is a closing argument with exhibits. Keep it. Frame it. Require everyone to recognize it.

The drive mattered because Lavaridge had been scoring. The Inferno reached the end zone on a 62-yard possession in the third quarter and a 67-yard possession in the fourth. Vermilion did not finish by trusting that the opponent would stop being productive. It finished by keeping the opponent away from the ball. There is a difference between hoping a lead survives and spending the remaining time making survival unnecessary.

Chandelure completed twenty of twenty-seven for 225 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions. He took no sacks. Swalot caught all six targets for 51 yards and a score; Whiscash added 61 receiving yards and Victreebel 46. Kangaskhan ran for 89 yards and caught a twenty-yard touchdown early in the fourth quarter. This was a productive offense, and the closing possession showed how that production could serve a purpose beyond improving a final stat line.
The flattering record does not explain the ugly week

One week earlier, Vermilion lost 34–10 to a Fortree team that had not won. Rowan dropped the Volts five places, to thirteenth, and pointed to a plus-one point differential. The victory over Lavaridge improved that figure to plus-eight. It also provided a response worth acknowledging. What it did not provide was a certificate declaring the Fortree result an administrative error.

When a team wins six of eight, people become very eager to call every difficult moment resilience. Sometimes it is. Sometimes it is a narrow margin that will not remain narrow in the helpful direction. I am not assigning a mathematical destiny to Vermilion. I am asking for the offense and defense to create a larger cushion before the next opponent discovers the same weaknesses Fortree found. That request seems considerably less insulting than pretending nothing needs attention.

The injuries are part of the explanation. Both Exploud running backs remain unavailable, with eleven weeks listed for number 87 and four for number 31. Tentacruel is out three weeks at corner, while Delcatty has eleven remaining. Those absences cannot be dismissed by shouting the record more loudly. They also cannot become an all-purpose excuse for every result. The available players produced 312 yards against Lavaridge and kept the ball for the last four minutes. There is evidence of a workable offense in the same week as the limitations.

The defense supplied three sacks, all described in the opening quarter's play log, and held Lavaridge to one successful third down in six attempts. It also allowed those two second-half touchdown drives. I can applaud the early pressure and question the later resistance without changing my mind halfway through a sentence. The team contains both. The second half of the season will be less forgiving if the Volts keep offering the opponent a choice between them.
The star and the supporting work

Drakloak leads the league with 755 receiving yards. That is a first-half distinction worthy of more attention than Vermilion's uneasy arithmetic usually allows. It is also a season total, not a reason to invent receiving production for him in this particular game. The Week 9 box score puts the catches with Swalot, Whiscash, Victreebel and the other contributors. The Volts won through the players who actually performed the work that afternoon.

That distinction is useful for the larger argument. A team with a major individual receiving story still needs a complete offense when a different set of names supplies the decisive catches. Vermilion had one against Lavaridge. Six completions on six targets for Swalot, including the third-down catch that kept the last drive alive, were more immediately valuable than any discussion of who leads the season chart. A star can draw attention. The next first down must still be earned by whoever gets the ball.

Sootopolis is next, away from home. The Surge are 3–5 after losing 35–7 at Saffron, and they managed twenty-two rushing yards in that defeat. Vermilion should see an opportunity to control the game. It should also remember what happened the last time an opponent's poor record was allowed to do the talking before kickoff. The schedule does not award a win for recognizing that the other team has problems.

Six wins are a fine place to begin the second half. A plus-eight differential is an excellent reason to keep working. I am not asking Lt. Surge to surrender the record, and I am not interested in a ceremonial apology for having it. I am asking for more of the possession that ended this game: useful catches, sustained movement, and an opponent left waiting. That is a serious team's behavior. Do it often enough, and the numbers will stop requiring so much explanation.
